title: Plant transport: xylem and transpiration; Human impact and sustainability; Experimental design and variables
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PR01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t2 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t3 term and clue written for the game; PR01a#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX10a#N.4, PR01a#N.2b, EX10a#N.12c, PR01a#N.6, PR01a#N.8.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Independent variable
items.clue: The one factor the experimenter changes on purpose.

items.label: Negative control
items.clue: Set-up in which no effect is expected, such as one using a boiled enzyme.

items.label: Positive control
items.clue: Set-up in which an effect is known to occur, showing the method can detect one.

items.label: Null hypothesis
items.clue: States that the factor being changed has no effect, or that there is no difference.

questions.stem: During a summer, a large tree takes up thousands of liters of water from the soil through its roots. Which statement best describes what happens to most of this water?

options.text: Most of it stays stored in the tree's wood and leaves for the rest of its life.
Most of it evaporates from its leaves and returns to the air as vapor.
Most of it is built into the sugars and the new wood that the tree makes.
Most of it is used up inside the tree's cells and then ceases to exist.

questions.explanation: Most of the water absorbed by the roots moves up through the plant and evaporates from the leaves (transpiration), returning to the atmosphere. Only a small fraction is held in the tree's tissues or used in photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Researchers test the hypothesis that competition for food limits the number of offspring produced per beetle in a hypothetical species of flour beetle. They place 10, 20, 40 or 80 adult beetles in identical containers, each holding 20 g of flour as food, and count the offspring produced per adult beetle after 30 days. Which is the independent variable?

options.text: The mass of flour supplied as food in every container
The offspring produced per adult beetle by day 30
The length of time, 30 days, before offspring were counted
The starting number of adults put in each container

questions.stem: In a tall tree on a sunny day, water evaporates from the leaves and the whole column of water in the xylem moves upward. Which statement best explains how the water reaches the top without a pump?

options.text: Root cells pump water into the xylem using ATP, and this pressure pushes the column all the way up.
Evaporation from the leaves pulls the water column, and cohesion holds it together as it rises.
Water climbs the narrow xylem vessels by capillary action alone, which can lift it to any height.
The tree takes in most of its water through its leaves, from rain and dew, so the water never has to rise.

questions.stem: A student plans to test whether the number of double bonds in a fatty acid affects its melting point, using fatty acids with 0, 1, 2 and 3 double bonds that all have the same chain length. Which statement is an appropriate null hypothesis for this investigation?

options.text: Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at lower temperatures than those with fewer.
Fatty acids with more double bonds will melt at higher temperatures than those with fewer.
The number of double bonds in a fatty acid has no effect on its melting point.
None of the fatty acids will melt at any of the temperatures used in the investigation.

questions.stem: A filter-paper disc soaked in catalase solution sinks in hydrogen peroxide and rises when enough oxygen has formed on it. In 1% hydrogen peroxide the disc took 50 s to rise; in 2% it took 20 s. Which statement about the reaction rate is correct?

options.text: Rate is proportional to 1/time, so the rate at 2% (0.05 s⁻¹) is 2.5 times the rate at 1% (0.02 s⁻¹).
The rate at 1% is 50 and at 2% is 20, so the rate fell when the concentration was doubled.
Doubling the concentration doubles the rate, so the rate at 2% is 0.04 s⁻¹, twice that at 1%.
The rate cannot be found, because the volume of oxygen produced was not measured in either trial.
